characters.description: Chicago's wizard and Warden, enjoying a rare stretch of quiet - which ends when the Queen of Winter comes to collect. Harry still owes Mab two favors from an old bargain, and the one she calls in drops him between the Winter and Summer Courts, the city's underworld, and the return of the worst enemies he has: the Knights of the Blackened Denarius. Something is also subtly wrong with his own magic, a gap he cannot quite see - and working out who arranged that, and why, is part of the game.
characters.name: Harry Dresden

characters.description: The Queen of the Winter Court, holder of two favors Harry has owed since she bought his debt years ago. Mab appears in person to call in the second: Harry will act as her Emissary and protect - of all people - John Marcone. Her motives, as always, are layered beneath centuries of ice; she gives Harry neither reasons nor mercy, and some of her help arrives in forms that look, until the last moment, exactly like sabotage.
characters.name: Mab

characters.description: Sergeant Karrin Murphy, Harry's partner in everything the law has no words for. She works the Marcone abduction from the mortal side, walks knowingly into a war between fallen angels and faerie queens, and in the book's darkest hour proves - in a way that surprises everyone, herself included - exactly what kind of person can hold a holy blade.
characters.name: Karrin Murphy

characters.description: Chicago's crime lord - recently become the first ordinary mortal to sign the Unseelie Accords as a freeholding lord, making him a recognized power among the supernatural nations. When he is taken from a fortified panic room by enemies who went through his defenses like paper, his abduction is the small favor of the title: Mab wants him found and protected, and Harry has to swallow years of enmity to do it. Even as a prisoner, Marcone plays a cold, disciplined long game.
characters.name: John Marcone

characters.description: Marcone's security consultant: a tall, blonde, terrifyingly capable woman who is far more than human - a valkyrie on contract from Monoc Securities. Gard's professional loyalty to Marcone survives his abduction, and her knowledge of the powers in play, her runes, and her axe make her one of the most valuable allies in the hunt for her employer.
characters.name: Sigrun Gard

characters.description: Knight of the Cross, bearer of Amoracchius, Harry's oldest ally in the war against the Denarians - and a father and husband whose family has already paid dearly for his calling. When Nicodemus and the coins return, Michael takes the field with his usual unshakable faith. The question that has always hung over the Knights - how far God's protection extends, and what happens when the plan requires a sacrifice - has never pressed harder than it does in this book.
characters.name: Michael Carpenter

characters.description: The agnostic Russian Knight of the Cross, bearer of Esperacchius, cheerful in the face of horrors that would break most soldiers. Sanya arrives to stand with Michael and Harry against the Denarians he once served, bringing his rifle, his good humor, and his firsthand understanding of what the coins do to the people who carry them.
characters.name: Sanya

characters.description: The Archive - the living sum of everything humanity has ever written - still vested in a small, solemn girl whom Harry calls Ivy. Bound to absolute neutrality, she is summoned to preside over a formal parley under the Accords when the Denarian crisis becomes a matter between nations. Her power is oceanic; her situation - one child, neutral, alone, and unique - is precisely the kind of thing an enemy who thinks in millennia knows how to exploit.
characters.name: The Archive

characters.description: The Archive's bodyguard, the mercenary who has kept her alive through everything her office attracts. Kincaid fights the book's battles with his usual meticulous, inhuman competence, and his bond with his young charge - gruff, unsentimental, and absolute - is tested by the worst thing that has ever happened on his watch.
characters.name: Kincaid

characters.description: The two-thousand-year-old leader of the Order of the Blackened Denarius, back in Chicago with his wife Tessa, his daughter Deirdre, and a full muster of coin-bound fallen angels. Nicodemus abducted Marcone as an opening move in a scheme aimed at a far greater prize, and he negotiates, betrays, and murders with the genial patience of a man who has been winning for twenty centuries. The noose at his throat remains one of the few things in creation that can hurt him.
characters.name: Nicodemus Archleone

characters.description: Harry's apprentice, whose subtle magic - veils and senses - now has real polish, and whose greatest contribution to this case is noticing something everyone else missed: a precise, surgical absence in Harry's own behavior. Molly stays largely behind the lines of the book's battles, but her perception changes the course of the endgame.
characters.name: Molly Carpenter

characters.description: A quiet man pushing a mop in a hospital corridor, who turns out to be something else entirely: Uriel, an archangel, appearing to Harry in the aftermath of the book's battles. Softly spoken and precise about the limits of what he may do, he confirms the nature of the new silver-white fire that has crept into Harry's magic, and leaves Harry with the sense that the war he can see is a small corner of a much larger one.
characters.name: Uriel

recaps.ending: The Denarians' true target was never Marcone: the abduction was the opening move of a scheme to capture the Archive, and at the Accords parley they take Ivy after a devastating battle. Harry answers with an assault on the Denarians' island stronghold in Lake Michigan, alongside Michael, Sanya, Murphy, Kincaid and Luccio. Mab returns what she had secretly taken - Harry's blasting rod, veiled from his own memory along with his fire magic - and Harry burns the enemy's position down around them. Ivy and Marcone are recovered alive; a number of Denarians are killed and several of their coins captured; Nicodemus, half-strangled with his own noose, survives through his daughter Deirdre and escapes; Tessa escapes as well. In the battle Murphy takes up the holy sword Fidelacchius, which blazes for her, though she declines its calling. The victory's price is Michael: gunned down during the extraction, he survives only barely and is left too badly maimed to fight again - his sword, Amoracchius, passes into Harry's keeping alongside Fidelacchius, and Michael retires to his family with a serenity Harry cannot fathom. In a hospital corridor the archangel Uriel, wearing a janitor's clothes, confirms what has changed in Harry: the death of Lasciel's shadow left space that has filled with soulfire, Heaven's counterpart to hellfire, fueled by Harry's own soul. Mab's second favor is paid, one remains, Marcone stands as an Accords lord with his debts to Harry unresolved, and Ivy - saved by a wizard who refused to write her off as an office - has a friend for the first time.
recaps.in_short: Mab calls in the second of Harry's three favors: act as Winter's Emissary and protect John Marcone, newly a freeholding lord under the Accords and abducted from a panic room by the returned Knights of the Blackened Denarius. As Summer inexplicably sends its goat-legged gruff assassins after Harry and his own fire magic has somehow gone missing from his mind, Harry hunts Nicodemus through parleys and betrayals - and learns too late that Marcone was bait: the Denarians' real target is the Archive, the little girl Ivy, whom they seize at the Accords negotiation. Harry leads Michael, Sanya, Murphy, Kincaid and Luccio in an assault on the Denarians' island in Lake Michigan; Mab returns his blasting rod and the memory she had veiled, and the stronghold burns. Ivy and Marcone are saved, coins are captured, Nicodemus and Tessa escape - and Michael is shot down in the extraction, crippled out of his knighthood, his sword joining Fidelacchius in Harry's trust. Uriel reveals Harry's new silver fire is soulfire, one Winter favor remains, and Harry finishes the job having beaten the eldest gruff with a donut.

recaps.text: Previously: Harry Dresden broke a conspiracy inside the White Court that was murdering Chicago's minor practitioners, clearing his half-brother Thomas and leaving Lara Raith - the true power behind the White King - in his debt, while confirming that a hidden 'Black Council' arms its pawns with Outsider power through agents like the necromancer Cowl. The shadow of the fallen angel Lasciel, which had lived in Harry's mind since he grabbed her coin to save a child, chose to die shielding him, leaving his head silent. Harry trains Molly Carpenter as his apprentice under a shared death sentence; Murphy, demoted for standing with him, still runs his mortal-world flank. Of the three favors Harry once owed Mab, Queen of Winter, two remain. The holy sword Fidelacchius rests in his keeping. His enemies of record include Nicodemus Archleone and the coin-bound fallen angels of the Blackened Denarius - and crime lord John Marcone has just become the first mortal to sign the Unseelie Accords as a freeholding lord.

A snowball fight at the Carpenter home is interrupted by monsters out of a fairy tale: gruffs, the goat-legged soldiers of Summer, attacking Harry with military precision - and each wave that fails is followed by a bigger brother. Before Harry can work out why the Summer Court wants him dead, Winter answers the question's other half: Mab appears and calls in the second of his three favors. John Marcone has been abducted - taken from a fortified safe room by something that tore through his precautions - and Harry, as Winter's Emissary, is to find and protect him. The scene of the abduction shows Denarian handiwork, and Marcone's people, the valkyrie Gard and the enormous Hendricks, join the hunt for their employer. Harry also can't shake the feeling that something small is missing from his own habits, though he cannot name it.

The enemy shows its face: Nicodemus Archleone is back in Chicago with his wife Tessa, his daughter Deirdre, and more coin-bound Denarians than Harry has ever seen in one place - and because Marcone is a signatory of the Accords, his abduction is a matter between nations. A formal parley is convened, with the Archive - Ivy, the solemn little girl who is the sum of human written knowledge - summoned as neutral arbiter, her bodyguard Kincaid at her side. Michael and Sanya, the Knights of the Cross, take the field as the Denarians' oldest enemies. The negotiation at the Shedd Aquarium is a Denarian trap: the parley erupts into battle, and the enemy's design finally shows itself - the fallen angels' interest reaches past Marcone toward something far more valuable.

The aquarium battle costs the Denarians dearly but wins them their true prize: Ivy. The Archive - one small girl, neutral, unique, and irreplaceable - is taken, to be broken or claimed for the coins, and Kincaid is nearly killed failing to prevent it. Amid the wreckage Harry pieces the scheme together: Marcone was bait from the start, the parley a mechanism to bring the Archive within reach. Molly, meanwhile, has spotted the surgical absence in Harry's behavior - he has not used fire magic in weeks, his blasting rod is nowhere in his memory, and he never noticed: someone has been inside his head. Hunted by Summer's gruffs whenever he surfaces, bargaining with powers on every side, Harry locates the Denarians' stronghold - an island far out in Lake Michigan - and Nicodemus offers terms designed to cost Harry his soul either way. Harry chooses assault instead.

The strike force crosses the lake in the teeth of winter: Harry, Michael, Sanya, Murphy, Kincaid and Warden-Captain Luccio, against a fortified island held by fallen angels. In the battle's crux Mab returns what she had taken - the blasting rod, and the veiled memory of his own fire magic - and Harry understands the manipulation only as he turns it loose: his fire, hidden even from himself until the moment it could be decisive, burns the Denarians' position down around them. Ivy is pulled alive out of her captors' hands; Marcone is recovered; Denarians die and coins are taken. Nicodemus, choked with his own noose for the second time in his long life, is saved by Deirdre and escapes with Tessa. And in the extraction, gunfire finds Michael Carpenter, and the best man Harry knows goes down.

The bill comes due, and the accounting is strange. Michael survives - barely - but his body is ruined for war: his knighthood is over, and he accepts it with a peace that baffles Harry, going home to Charity and the children he now gets to grow old with; Amoracchius joins Fidelacchius in Harry's keeping, two swords waiting for bearers. Murphy, who took up Fidelacchius in the island battle and saw it blaze in her hands, declines the calling on her own terms. The eldest gruff, Summer's final and mightiest assassin, is defeated by the letter of faerie law and a donut - Harry's kind of victory. In a hospital corridor, a janitor who is the archangel Uriel confirms what the perceptive have noticed: the space where Lasciel's shadow died has filled with soulfire, the fire of Heaven, drawn from Harry's own soul. Mab's second favor is paid with one remaining; Marcone resumes his throne owing Harry his life; Ivy, guarded by a healing Kincaid, has gained the one thing the Archive was never permitted - a friend. The coins are locked away, but Tessa's escape and the design behind the whole affair promise the Denarians are not finished with Harry Dresden.

characters.description: A large, slow-seeming novice in the great Church of the god Om, in the theocratic nation of Omnia. Illiterate but gifted with a flawless memory that forgets nothing he has seen or heard, he is devout, literal-minded, and unfailingly kind. He tends the Citadel's melon garden, and is startled when a small tortoise begins to speak to him, claiming to be his god.
characters.name: Brutha

characters.description: The Great God Om, worshipped by millions across Omnia, who discovers to his horror that he has been reduced to a nearly powerless one-eyed tortoise. A god's strength depends on the number of people who truly believe in him rather than merely in his Church, and Om finds he has only one real believer left, the novice Brutha, the only person who can hear him. Blustering and self-centred, he must rely on Brutha simply to survive.
characters.name: Om

characters.description: A deacon of the Church and a leading figure in the Quisition, Omnia's feared apparatus for detecting and punishing heresy. Austere, patient, and utterly certain of his own righteousness, he wields terror as an instrument of faith and pursues power within the Church with cold single-mindedness. He takes an interest in Brutha's perfect memory.
characters.name: Vorbis

characters.description: A blind, cynical philosopher of Ephebe who lives in a barrel and carries a lantern, known for a plain-spoken, questioning outlook. He is the author of a book describing the world as a disc carried on the back of a great turtle, a view that is deep heresy in Omnia, which teaches that the world is a sphere.
characters.name: Didactylos

characters.description: The nephew and assistant of the philosopher Didactylos, a young man fascinated by machines and mechanisms. Practical where his uncle is contemplative, he applies philosophy to engineering and builds devices to solve problems.
characters.name: Urn

characters.description: A sergeant in the Omnian army who secretly leads an underground movement against the Church's tyranny. Hardened and angry at the cruelties of the Quisition, he wants to bring the whole oppressive structure down by force.
characters.name: Sergeant Simony

characters.description: An unassuming, elderly sweeper who moves quietly about the Citadel with a broom, easily overlooked and treated as a nobody. He is in fact far more than he appears, a member of an order that watches over the proper unfolding of history, and he keeps a discreet eye on events in Omnia.
characters.name: Lu-Tze

characters.description: The elderly novice-master of the Citadel, in charge of the young men in Brutha's dormitory. Set in his ways and given to muttering at the temptations he imagines everywhere, he oversees Brutha's early religious instruction.
characters.name: Brother Nhumrod

recaps.ending: Small Gods ends with the tyranny of Omnia's Church broken and a new, gentler order begun. At the point of Brutha's public execution, the Great God Om finally reclaims his strength: carried up by an eagle and dropped onto Deacon Vorbis, he kills the man who had seized control of the Church, and as the crowd sees Brutha's courage, true belief floods back to Om. Brutha survives and becomes the new prophet. Instead of wielding the power he inherits as his predecessors did, he strikes a new bargain with his god and remakes Omnia, abolishing the Quisition and steering the nation toward tolerance, literacy, and a lasting peace, while stopping the war Vorbis had provoked. The story then jumps a hundred years forward to Brutha's own death as an old man. When Death comes for him and he must cross the desert that lies beyond life, Brutha finds the spirit of Vorbis still standing there, alone and terrified, unmoved since his death because he had never truly cared for anyone but himself. Brutha takes Vorbis's hand and walks with him across the desert, choosing kindness toward his old enemy as his final act.
recaps.in_short: In the theocratic nation of Omnia, the Great God Om finds his power gone: because true belief, not mere Church membership, feeds a god, and only the kind, perfectly remembering novice Brutha genuinely believes in him, Om has shrunk to a nearly helpless talking tortoise. Brutha, the only one who can hear him, is taken into the service of Deacon Vorbis, a cold master of the Church's torturing Quisition, and travels with him to the philosopher-city of Ephebe, where forbidden ideas, including that the world is a disc on a turtle, begin to shake Brutha's unquestioning faith. Vorbis engineers treachery and war; after a shipwreck Brutha carries the injured Vorbis across the desert out of sheer decency. In Omnia, Vorbis makes himself prophet and condemns Brutha to death, but Om intervenes, dropped by an eagle onto Vorbis to kill him as belief and his power return. Brutha becomes prophet, ends the Quisition, and turns Omnia toward tolerance and peace. A century later, dying, he helps even Vorbis's frightened soul cross the desert of death.

recaps.text: In the theocratic nation of Omnia, whose powerful Church enforces worship of the Great God Om, a slow but kind novice named Brutha, blessed with a perfect memory, is astonished when a small one-eyed tortoise begins speaking to him and claims to be Om himself. Om has discovered a terrible truth: a god's power comes from genuine belief, and though millions attend his Church out of fear and habit, Brutha is the only person left who truly believes in him, which is why he has dwindled to a near-helpless tortoise able to speak to no one else. Brutha's gift for remembering everything draws the notice of Deacon Vorbis, a cold and formidable figure of the Quisition, the Church's machinery of inquisition and torture. Vorbis takes Brutha into his service and includes him in a diplomatic mission to the distant city of Ephebe.

The mission reaches Ephebe, a coastal city of philosophers and argument, utterly unlike rigid Omnia. There Brutha, carrying Om the tortoise with him, encounters thinkers such as the blind, barrel-dwelling philosopher Didactylos and his inventor nephew Urn. He is confronted by ideas forbidden at home, above all the claim that the world is a disc riding on a great turtle, which contradicts the Church's teaching that it is a sphere. Brutha, who has never questioned anything, begins to be troubled by what he learns and by the gap between his Church's cruelty and the god he actually hears. Vorbis, meanwhile, pursues his own designs behind the mission's official purpose.

Vorbis's true intentions surface as he engineers treachery to serve the Church's ambitions, turning the diplomatic errand toward conflict between Omnia and Ephebe. In the upheaval Brutha, Vorbis, and Om flee Ephebe by sea, but their vessel is wrecked and they are cast into the desert. There Brutha, out of simple decency, carries the injured and helpless Vorbis across the burning wasteland on his back, keeping alive the man who embodies everything cruel about his Church. Om, still a vulnerable tortoise dependent on Brutha, is carried along, and Brutha's steady kindness under extremity marks him as something the Church never made him.

Back in Omnia, Vorbis consolidates his power and has himself installed as the Church's new prophet and supreme head, staging events to confirm his authority. Brutha, whose growing conscience and knowledge make him dangerous, is condemned as a heretic and prepared for public execution, to be tortured to death on an iron instrument before the assembled faithful. Om, still nearly powerless, is desperate to save his one believer but can do almost nothing in his tortoise form. The confrontation between Brutha's plain goodness and Vorbis's ruthless certainty comes to a head before the crowds of the Citadel.

At the climax Om finally acts: he arranges to be carried aloft by an eagle and dropped from a great height onto Vorbis, killing him, and as the crowd witnesses Brutha's courage and the god's returning power, real belief surges back and Om is restored to strength. Brutha survives and becomes the new prophet of Omnia. Rather than continue the Church's tyranny, he negotiates a new understanding with Om, ending the Quisition and turning Omnia toward tolerance, learning, and peace, and he halts the war that Vorbis's schemes had set in motion. The book closes many years later: Brutha dies as an old man, and Death comes for him. In the desert that souls must cross, Brutha finds the terrified spirit of Vorbis, who has stood alone and frightened there ever since his death, and takes him by the hand to help him make the journey, returning kindness for cruelty one last time.

characters.description: The head of Moscow Centre's special directorate, the Soviet officer who ran the agent that destroyed the Circus and who has been Smiley's opponent for twenty years. He is known to the British only by a work name, a photograph and a career reconstructed from fragments: ascetic, unbribable, and safe from the ordinary levers because he appears to want nothing for himself. Smiley met him once, years ago, in an Indian jail, tried to turn him and failed, and gave him a cigarette lighter belonging to his wife.
characters.name: Karla

characters.description: A Russian emigree living in modest circumstances in Paris, ageing, unwell and alone, who left the Soviet Union many years ago and had to leave a daughter behind. She is approached in a cafe by a Soviet official who offers, on conditions, to have the girl allowed out to join her. Suspicious of the offer and of the papers she is asked to sign, she writes for advice to the leader of an emigre organisation she trusted long ago.
characters.name: Maria Ostrakova

characters.description: The Soviet official who approaches Ostrakova in Paris: nominally a trade or embassy functionary, effusive, sweating and oddly clumsy for a man on such an errand. He talks a great deal more than his business requires.
characters.name: Oleg Kirov

characters.description: An elderly Estonian, once a soldier and a Soviet officer and for decades afterwards the leader of a Baltic emigre group in London, run for years as a Circus agent and then dropped when the service reorganised. Poor, proud and still observing the tradecraft he was taught, he telephones his old service demanding to speak to the case officer he knew by a work name, insists on meeting under Moscow rules, and says he has something that concerns them all.
characters.name: General Vladimir

characters.description: Long retired from the Circus, living alone in Chelsea and sorting his papers, still married in name to Ann and still without her. He is fetched out at night to deal with the death of a former agent, on the understanding that his job is to tidy the matter away quietly. He is old, tired and out of practice, and the one man who understands what the dead man was trying to say.
characters.name: George Smiley

characters.description: Smiley's wife, absent, living elsewhere with someone else, and still the fixed point of his private life. Her cigarette lighter and her infidelities both belong to the history that binds Smiley to his opponent.
characters.name: Ann Smiley

characters.description: The Cabinet Office official responsible for the intelligence services, anxious above all that an emigre killing in London should not become a political embarrassment. He wants the affair closed with a minimum of enquiry and turns to Smiley because Smiley can be disowned.
characters.name: Oliver Lacon

characters.description: A senior Circus administrator of the present regime, protective of procedure, budgets and his own position, who treats the dead man as an obsolete liability and Smiley as an awkwardness to be managed.
characters.name: Lauder Strickland

characters.description: A very young Circus duty officer who took the old man's telephone call and, having been taught nothing about the people the service used to run, handled it by the book. He is shaken by what followed and tells Smiley more than he is supposed to.
characters.name: Mostyn

characters.description: An Estonian exile who runs a Baltic emigre library and club in London, once the General's deputy and now the keeper of his organisation's dwindling affairs. Talkative, aggrieved and a considerable chess player, he gives his own version of the old man's last weeks.
characters.name: Mikhel

characters.description: A young Estonian lorry driver on the continental routes, the son of one of the General's old comrades, who ran errands for the old man out of family loyalty and without understanding what he was carrying. He is frightened and wants nothing more to do with any of it.
characters.name: Villem

characters.description: The Circus's former Soviet researcher, now seriously ill and living in the Norfolk countryside with her companion and her dogs, drinking and remembering. Her memory for Moscow Centre's people and their careers is still complete, and she has never stopped following the career of one officer in particular.
characters.name: Connie Sachs

characters.description: A stateless adventurer of Baltic origin, sometime prisoner, confidence man and agent for several services, who worked with the General for years. Charming, unreliable and physically brave, he lives in Hamburg and has been chasing a particular Soviet official for reasons of his own.
characters.name: Otto Leipzig

characters.description: A former Circus officer, now dealing in pictures in the West End under an assumed name and a foreign accent. Hungarian, adaptable and expert in surveillance and safe houses, he owes Smiley his freedom from prosecution and comes back to run a team for him without asking what the operation is for.
characters.name: Toby Esterhase

characters.description: A Hamburg nightclub proprietor and old associate of Otto Leipzig, discreet, businesslike and loyal to his friend. He keeps what Leipzig left with him and will hand it over only on the right terms.
characters.name: Claus Kretzschmar

characters.description: The commercial counsellor at the Soviet embassy in Bern, a pedantic, henpecked official with an academic manner, a wife who watches him and a mistress among the embassy staff. He performs, under orders from Moscow, a private duty outside all normal embassy business, and he is very frightened of it.
characters.name: Grigoriev

characters.description: A young Russian woman in a private Swiss clinic, disturbed, articulate and intermittently violent, held under a name and a nationality that are not hers. She does not know who is paying for her, and the accounts she gives of her own history contradict one another.
characters.name: Alexandra

recaps.ending: Grigoriev, broken by Toby's team and questioned by Smiley in a Bern safe flat, gives up the whole arrangement: the girl in the clinic is Karla's daughter, mentally ill, smuggled out of Russia under a false identity and a false nationality, and maintained in Switzerland with money embezzled from Moscow Centre's operational funds. Kirov was ordered to build the legend, talked too much to Otto Leipzig, and was recalled and shot; Vladimir, Leipzig and very nearly Ostrakova were killed to bury the same secret. Smiley now has what no professional lever could give him: the private crime for which Karla's own service would destroy him. He sends word to Moscow through the channel Karla built, offering him the choice between exposure and coming across. Karla comes. On a bridge in Berlin, watched by Smiley, Toby and the reception party, he crosses into the West, a small man carrying almost nothing, and as he passes he drops the cigarette lighter Smiley once gave him. Smiley has beaten him by using the one human attachment Karla had, exactly as Karla would have done, and the victory gives him nothing. He turns away, and when Toby tells him he has won he can barely agree.
recaps.in_short: In Paris an ageing Russian emigree, Ostrakova, is approached by a Soviet official offering to release the daughter she left behind, and writes for help to General Vladimir, an old Estonian exile in London and a discarded Circus agent. Vladimir tries to reach his former case officer under Moscow rules and is shot dead on Hampstead Heath. Smiley, long retired, is sent to tidy the death away quietly, and instead follows the trail the old man left: a hidden negative, an emigre courier, a Hamburg confidence man named Otto Leipzig, and photographs and a tape recording of the Soviet official's indiscretions. Reassembling his old people, Connie Sachs, Toby Esterhase, Guillam and Mendel, and working outside the service, Smiley establishes that Karla, the head of Moscow Centre's special directorate, has been using Centre money and Centre officers to hide his mentally ill daughter in a Swiss clinic under a false identity. Everyone who learned of it has been killed. Smiley breaks the Soviet official who pays the clinic's bills, and uses the daughter to force Karla's defection. Karla crosses a Berlin bridge into the West, and Smiley takes no pleasure in it.

recaps.text: Previously: George Smiley spent his career in the Circus, Britain's secret intelligence service, and much of it against Karla, the head of Moscow Centre's special directorate. Karla recruited and ran Bill Haydon, who rose to the top of the Circus, betrayed its networks and its allies, wrecked the operation that left Jim Prideaux shot and imprisoned, and conducted an affair with Smiley's wife Ann on Karla's instructions to blunt Smiley's judgement. Brought back from retirement, Smiley identified and trapped Haydon and was left to rebuild the ruined service. Working backwards through what Haydon had suppressed, he then uncovered a Soviet payments operation in the Far East and traced it to Nelson Ko, an agent Karla had run inside China for twenty years; but the prize was taken over by the Americans and by Whitehall, the field man Jerry Westerby was killed, and Smiley was eased out of the chief's chair in favour of Saul Enderby. Smiley's marriage to Ann has not survived, and the two men's twenty-year contest has never been settled.

In Paris, Maria Ostrakova, an ageing Russian emigree, is approached in a cafe by a Soviet official who says her daughter Alexandra, left behind in Russia many years earlier, may be allowed to join her if she signs certain papers. The interview frightens her: the man knows too much about her history and too little about her daughter, and the arrangement smells of something other than compassion. She writes to General Vladimir, the leader of a Baltic emigre group in London whom she trusted long ago. Vladimir, an old Estonian long since dropped by the Circus, telephones his former service demanding to see the case officer he knew only by a work name, insists on meeting under Moscow rules, and says he has proof of something big. A young duty officer handles the call by the book. Before any meeting can take place, Vladimir is shot dead on Hampstead Heath at night, his face destroyed by the second bullet, and George Smiley is fetched out of retirement to identify the body.

Lacon of the Cabinet Office and the Circus administrator Strickland want the killing disposed of as an emigre quarrel with no British connection, and give Smiley an unofficial commission to make the loose ends disappear. Smiley does the opposite. Going over the old man's route and lodgings, he finds what the killers missed: a cigarette packet left in the classic manner with a photographic negative concealed in it, the proof Vladimir was carrying to his meeting. He interviews the young duty officer, who repeats the old man's words; and Mikhel, the deputy at the emigre library, whose account is fluent and incomplete. He learns that Vladimir had recently sent a young Estonian courier abroad. The service, meanwhile, formally wants nothing to do with any of it, which leaves Smiley free to work alone.

The courier, a lorry driver named Villem, admits to a run to Hamburg where a stranger passed him an envelope on a train. Smiley goes to Norfolk to see Connie Sachs, dying and drinking in the country, who identifies the men in the story: Otto Leipzig, a Baltic adventurer and part-time agent who had worked with Vladimir for years, and Oleg Kirov, a Soviet official whose career and postings make no sense unless he was doing something outside embassy work. Connie also confirms whose directorate Kirov belonged to. In Hamburg, Smiley finds that Leipzig has been murdered, but recovers from Leipzig's associate Kretzschmar what the operation was for: a compromising photograph and a tape on which Kirov, drunk and boastful, describes having been ordered to find a suitable emigre identity for a girl, a piece of work no intelligence service would ever run in that way.

Smiley recruits his own people rather than the Circus's: Toby Esterhase, now selling pictures in the West End, brings a surveillance team; Peter Guillam helps from Paris; Mendel does the London work. In Paris, Ostrakova, who has been living in fear since the approach, is run down in the street and badly hurt, and survives; Smiley finds her and hears her account of Kirov's proposition and of the daughter she has not seen since infancy. The pattern is now clear. Kirov was building a false identity in the West for a young woman, using an emigree mother as the cover story, and everyone who came near the secret has been killed: Kirov himself recalled to Moscow and shot, then Vladimir and Leipzig. The operation was not run by Moscow Centre as an institution but by one man inside it, using its resources for a purpose of his own, and the trail leads to Switzerland.

In Bern, Toby's team identifies the man who does the paying: Grigoriev, the Soviet embassy's commercial counsellor, a fussy, unhappy official who makes regular private journeys to a discreet clinic in the countryside and hands over large sums in cash. In the clinic is a disturbed young Russian woman, registered under a name and a nationality that are not hers, who does not know who is responsible for her. Smiley has the watchers document every movement, then has Grigoriev taken quietly and confronted in a safe flat with what has been observed: the money, the false papers, his mistress, and the certainty that his own service would treat all of it as a capital matter. Grigoriev, terrified and relieved to be able to speak, begins to explain who ordered him to do it and why.

Grigoriev's account completes the case: the girl in the clinic is Karla's own daughter, mentally ill, taken out of Russia under an invented identity and kept in Switzerland with money stolen from Moscow Centre's operational funds. It is the one act for which Karla's own service would destroy him, and it is why Kirov, Vladimir and Leipzig died and why Ostrakova was to have died. Smiley sends Karla the choice through the channel Karla himself built: come over, or be exposed to Moscow. Then he waits in Berlin. On a winter night Karla walks across the bridge into the West, a small, ordinary man carrying nothing, and as he passes Smiley he drops the cigarette lighter that Smiley had given him twenty years earlier in an Indian jail. Smiley has won by doing exactly what his opponent would have done, using a sick girl and a frightened official as instruments, and he leaves the bridge with no sense of triumph at all.

aliases: His Grace, the Duke of Ankh
characters.description: Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch and, by marriage, Duke of Ankh, a rank he has never become reconciled to. A copper by instinct and conviction, suspicious of privilege, including his own, and grimly aware of how much anger he keeps under control. He is a devoted, awkward father who reads his small son a bedtime story every night without fail, and he is about to be removed from the city and the job for the first time in his adult life.
characters.name: Sam Vimes

characters.description: The Patrician of Ankh-Morpork, who governs by knowing exactly what people will do and arranging matters accordingly. He has taken an interest in the idea of Commander Vimes being sent somewhere with no crime in it.
characters.name: Lord Vetinari

characters.description: Vimes's wife: an aristocrat by birth, a dragon breeder by enthusiasm, and immovable once she has decided what is good for her family. She has inherited a large country estate and has determined that her husband is going to take a holiday on it.
characters.name: Lady Sybil

characters.description: Vimes's six-year-old son, cheerful, observant, and currently engrossed in a natural history of animal droppings, a subject he can discuss at any length and in any company.
characters.name: Young Sam

characters.description: The Vimes household's gentleman's gentleman: impeccably correct, quietly amused, and equipped with a past on the streets that he has never entirely put down. He carries useful things in his hat and is a great deal more dangerous than any butler needs to be.
characters.name: Willikins

characters.description: The landlord of the village pub, an incomer with a professional welcome and a very good memory for faces, who recognizes Vimes rather faster than a country publican should. He knows a good deal about what happens locally and is careful about which parts of it he mentions.
characters.name: Jiminy

characters.description: A retired officer among the local gentry, straight-backed, courteous, and rather more troubled by the district's arrangements than his neighbours are. He has old-fashioned ideas about honour that his acquaintances find inconvenient.
characters.name: Colonel Makepeace

characters.description: The young local chief constable, the third generation of his family to hold the post, with no training, no colleagues, and a rule book he has largely worked out for himself. Earnest, badly out of his depth, and braver than his situation deserves.
characters.name: Feeney Upshot

characters.description: A goblin who attaches himself to Vimes: filthy, evil-smelling, sardonic, and entirely unbothered by either fact. He knows the country, the caves, and the river better than anyone alive, and turns up whenever Vimes is about to need him.
characters.name: Stinky

characters.description: A writer of children's books who lives locally and is regarded by the county as an eccentric. She has spent years among the goblins, has learned their language and their beliefs, and teaches those who will learn, which the neighbourhood considers at best foolish.
characters.name: Miss Felicity Beedle

characters.description: A young goblin woman living in the caves above the estate, taught music by Miss Beedle, who plays the harp with a skill that is impossible to explain away. What she can do is an argument in itself about what goblins are.
characters.name: Tears of the Mushroom

characters.description: A local man who works as an enforcer for people with money: fast, capable, and entirely without hesitation, and unusual even among killers in that he seems to feel nothing about it at all.
characters.name: Stratford

characters.description: A veteran Ankh-Morpork Watch sergeant of limited ambition and considerable seniority, who handles an item of goblin property in the course of a routine inquiry and begins, slowly and frighteningly, to stop being himself.
characters.name: Sergeant Colon

characters.description: A six-inch-tall Watch officer who was raised by gnomes and does the jobs no full-sized copper can, going into places nobody thinks to guard. He is a formidable fighter and is beginning to have questions about where he actually came from.
characters.name: Wee Mad Arthur

recaps.ending: Vimes proves the case: local landowners, with money and a name behind them, have been shipping goblins abroad as slave labour for the tobacco plantations and running smuggled goods on the same boats, and a young goblin woman was murdered to keep it quiet. Stratford, the killer, makes a last attempt on Vimes and on his family, and is taken; the aristocrat who financed the trade is dealt with by Vetinari on terms that leave him with nothing. The captured goblins are freed, Sergeant Colon recovers once the goblin pot he was carrying is returned to its owners, and the young country constable Feeney Upshot finishes the case as a real policeman with a future in the Watch. The decisive stroke is not an arrest: at a concert in Ankh-Morpork's Opera House, in front of the city's wealthy and powerful, Tears of the Mushroom plays the harp, and an audience that had always been told goblins were vermin sits and listens to one make music. On the strength of that, and of the case Vimes has built, the law changes and goblins become people, with the rights that follow. Vimes goes home to the city and the job, having taken the only holiday of his life and turned it, as everyone including his wife expected, into police work.
recaps.in_short: Sam Vimes, Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch and reluctant Duke of Ankh, is made to take a holiday at his wife's country estate, where he finds that a copper is still a copper. The district's goblins are treated as vermin, which under local law they are, and a young goblin woman has been murdered. The local chief constable, a young man named Feeney Upshot, arrests Vimes for it; Vimes turns him into a deputy instead, and together they uncover a trade run by the county's own gentry, shipping goblins abroad as slaves and smuggling goods on the return leg, with a professional killer named Stratford enforcing it. Vimes pursues the boats downriver through a flood, is nearly killed, and brings the evidence and the survivors back. The case ends not only in arrests but in a change of the law: at a concert in Ankh-Morpork a goblin girl plays the harp for the city's rich and powerful, and goblins are recognized as people. Vimes returns to the city with his family, his holiday having gone exactly as everyone expected.

recaps.text: Previously, in earlier books: Sam Vimes rose from a drunken night watchman to Commander of the Ankh-Morpork City Watch, rebuilding it into a large mixed force of humans, dwarfs, trolls, werewolves, and others, and became Duke of Ankh through his marriage to the aristocratic Lady Sybil Ramkin, a title he has never enjoyed. He answers, grudgingly, to Lord Vetinari, the Patrician, who finds him useful precisely because he cannot be bought or flattered. Vimes distrusts privilege, especially his own, polices by the principle that the law applies to everybody or it is not the law, and keeps a tight hold on his own temper because he knows what is underneath it. During an earlier case an ancient dwarfish thing got into his head and has remained there since, watching, as a kind of unwelcome guardian. He and Sybil have a young son, and Vimes's fiercest personal rule is that he is home to read to the boy at six o'clock.

Vimes is manoeuvred by his wife, with Lord Vetinari's approval, into taking the first holiday of his adult life: a stay at the Ramkin family's country estate, along with Lady Sybil, six-year-old Young Sam, and Willikins. The countryside receives him as a duke, which he loathes, and he discovers immediately that he does not know how to stop being a policeman. He notices the things the locals no longer see: the careful way people talk around certain subjects, the deference that goes slightly wrong, and the goblins who live in the hills above the estate and are regarded by everybody as vermin, which under the law here is exactly what they are.

Vimes explores the village and its pub, where the landlord recognizes him faster than any country publican should. He meets the local gentry at dinner and finds them polite, incurious, and united in the view that goblins are pests to be cleared. Young Sam, meanwhile, has fallen in love with a local children's author's book about animal droppings and pursues the subject relentlessly. Vimes takes note of a young local man who talks to him about the goblins and then is not seen again, and of the fact that nobody appears to consider this worth reporting. The country grows quietly more hostile the longer he asks questions, and the smell of a crime he cannot yet name settles over the whole estate.

Vimes finds the body of a young goblin woman who has been beaten to death. Under local law this is not murder, because a goblin is not a person, and the district has no intention of treating it as one. Feeney Upshot, the young and entirely untrained chief constable, arrives and arrests Vimes for the killing; Vimes, who could have stopped him, allows it, then takes charge of both the arrest and the constable, and begins turning him into a real policeman. Back in Ankh-Morpork the Watch has picked up a goblin item as evidence, and Sergeant Colon, who has handled it, is being slowly and frighteningly taken over by whatever is bound up in it. Vimes starts building a case in a place where the local magistrates, the local money, and the local law are all on the other side.

Vimes goes up into the goblin caves and learns what the district has been careful not to know: the goblins have a religion, a language, a craft, and a rigorous moral code, and one young goblin woman, taught by the local children's author, plays the harp well enough to settle the question of what goblins are for anyone honest enough to listen. The reason for the murder becomes clear as the trade behind it surfaces: goblins have been rounded up and shipped abroad as slave labour for the tobacco plantations, with smuggled goods carried on the return trips, organized and financed by people with land, titles, and friends. Enforcing it is Stratford, a local killer who works without hesitation or feeling, and who now knows that the Duke of Ankh is asking questions.

With Feeney beside him and a goblin guide who knows every inch of the country, Vimes goes after the boats carrying the captured goblins downriver. A storm turns into a flood, and the pursuit becomes a night run down a rising river that no sane person would attempt, ending with Vimes half drowned and washed up a long way from anywhere. In the city, Wee Mad Arthur works the docks and the warehouses from angles nobody thinks to guard, following the smuggled goods back to the people paying for them, and turns up an unexpected fact about his own origins along the way. Vimes survives, catches up with the boats, and takes them, and the surviving goblins are freed and, for the first time, in the hands of somebody prepared to treat what was done to them as a crime.

The pursuit ends downriver at Quirm, where Vimes, filthy and exhausted, hands over prisoners, evidence, and a case, and is put back together by the local Watch and eventually by his wife. Stratford, however, is not among those taken, and is loose and moving. Vimes returns to the estate and then to Ankh-Morpork with everything he needs: witnesses, documents, the boats, and the survivors. Sergeant Colon is freed of what he was carrying once the goblin property is returned to the people it belongs to. Feeney, having done everything asked of him and rather more, is no longer a village constable in anything but title, and the question is no longer whether the crime can be proved but whether a court will accept that a crime against goblins is a crime at all.

The case moves to the city, where the law, not the arrests, is the real battleground: everything Vimes has depends on goblins being people, and at present they legally are not. Vetinari, who has been several steps ahead throughout, arranges the occasion for settling it, a concert at the Opera House before an audience of the city's wealthiest and most influential. Vimes prepares the evidence, Miss Beedle prepares her pupil, and the aristocratic families behind the trade prepare to brazen it out. Stratford, who has nothing left to lose, makes his own preparations, and they involve Vimes's household.

At the Opera House, Tears of the Mushroom plays the harp in front of the city's rich and powerful, and an audience raised to believe goblins were vermin listens to one make music. That, together with the case Vimes has built, is enough: the law is changed and goblins become people, with everything that follows from it. Stratford makes his last attempt, going after Vimes and his family, and is taken; the estate is set alight in the course of it. The aristocrat who financed the slaving trade is dealt with by Vetinari on terms that strip him of everything, the freed goblins are given standing and protection, Sergeant Colon recovers, and Feeney Upshot ends the affair as a genuine policeman with a career in front of him. Vimes goes home to Ankh-Morpork with his wife and son, having taken the only holiday of his life and turned it, exactly as everyone expected, into police work.

characters.description: A gentle, determined girl in the same rigidly controlled community from the start of the series, assigned the role of Birthmother, or Vessel, to produce infants for the society. She is only fourteen when she bears her first child. Unlike others around her, she is not fully numbed to feeling, and she forms a fierce, forbidden attachment to the son she was never meant to know. That love becomes the driving purpose of her life.
characters.name: Claire

characters.description: Claire's infant son, the baby she bears in the controlled community and is forbidden to keep. In that society children are assigned to family units, and this small, restless infant does not thrive on its rigid schedule. He is the child at the center of Claire's search, and the thread that ties her story to the wider world of the series.
characters.name: Gabe

characters.description: A young man, known from earlier in the series, who once fled the controlled community as a boy carrying an infant to safety and later became the wise leader of a welcoming settlement. He is marked by pale eyes and a gift for perception. Claire's search will eventually cross paths with the community he guides.
characters.name: Jonas

characters.description: A young man in a remote, isolated settlement, patient and kind, who helps Claire rebuild her strength and teaches her the difficult skill of climbing the steep cliff that walls the village off from the world beyond. He bears the marks of a hard past of his own and understands, better than most, the danger of wanting something badly enough to pay any price for it.
characters.name: Einar

characters.description: A smooth, sinister figure who offers people the thing they most desire in exchange for something of themselves, always at a hidden and ruinous cost. He deals in longing and weakness, and his bargains bind those who accept them. He is the shadow that has moved through the wider world of the series, and he stands between Claire and what she seeks.
characters.name: Trademaster

characters.description: A young woman known from earlier in the series, born with a twisted leg and gifted at weaving, who once uncovered the lies of her harsh home village and chose to work for change. She is now part of the wider community of settlements where much of the later story unfolds.
characters.name: Kira

recaps.ending: Claire's long search ends at the community led by the pale-eyed young man from the start of the series, where her son Gabe has grown into a teenager, ignorant that his mother is the frail, prematurely aged woman who has arrived among them. Her age is the price she paid the Trademaster to complete her journey. Gabe comes to understand who she is and discovers that he possesses a rare gift of his own, the ability to send his mind into another person. He seeks out the Trademaster and confronts him directly. Rather than fighting with force, Gabe uses his gift to make the Trademaster confront his own name and the hollow, joyless nature of what he is, and this recognition destroys him. With the villain undone, the bargain that stole Claire's youth is broken and she is made whole and young again. Mother and son are reunited, and the quartet closes on the linked communities at peace, the long harm of the controlled society and the Trademaster's cruelty finally answered.
recaps.in_short: Claire is a fourteen-year-old Birthmother in the rigidly controlled community of the series' opening, who bears a son through a difficult surgery and is quietly reassigned to other work. Unnumbed to feeling, she becomes fixated on the boy, Gabe, and when the infant is spirited out of the community to save his life, she is separated from him by a disaster at sea. Washed ashore with no memory in a remote cliffbound village, she slowly recovers, and once she learns she is a mother searching for her child, she trains for years to climb out and follow him. To complete her journey she strikes a bargain with the sinister Trademaster, trading away her youth, and arrives aged and weakened at the welcoming settlement where Gabe, now a young man, has grown up under the wise Leader. Gabe discovers his own gift for entering others' minds, confronts Trademaster, and destroys him by forcing him to face his own emptiness. With the villain undone, the bargain is broken, Claire is restored, and mother and son are reunited at last.

recaps.text: Earlier in the series: A boy named Jonas, chosen to hold his controlled community's suppressed memories, learned the truth about its comforts and cruelties and fled with an infant to save the baby's life, reaching a gentler world. In a separate harsh village, an orphaned girl named Kira, gifted at weaving, exposed her rulers' lies and stayed to work for change. In a welcoming community called Village, a young messenger named Matty, who could pass through the surrounding Forest, gave his life to heal the land when the community's hearts hardened and the Forest turned deadly; Jonas now leads that world of linked settlements. This story returns to the beginning, to the controlled community, and to the mother of the infant Jonas once carried to safety.

In the rigidly ordered community of the series' opening, a girl named Claire has been assigned the role of Birthmother, producing infants for a society that assigns children to family units and dulls its people to strong feeling. At only fourteen she bears a son through a difficult birth that requires surgery, and afterward she is quietly reassigned to different work. Because the process left her without the usual numbing routine, Claire is not as deadened as those around her, and she finds herself drawn with dangerous intensity toward the child she was never meant to know or keep. That secret, forbidden love begins to shape everything she will do.

characters.description: A sixteen-year-old boarder at the Quirm College for Young Ladies, orphaned when her parents died in a coach accident. Relentlessly practical and unimpressed by anything that cannot be demonstrated, she has always been able to do things she has never questioned: people forget she is there when she wants them to, and doors are not always an obstacle. She has a white streak in her hair and a habit of asking exactly the question nobody wants asked. She has never been told who her grandfather is.
characters.name: Susan Sto Helit

characters.description: The anthropomorphic personification of death, a robed skeleton who collects the souls of the dying and speaks in a voice that arrives inside the head. Curious about the living for far longer than is good for him, he has taken a family, an apprentice and a granddaughter, and he remembers everything, permanently and in full. Faced with a loss he cannot accept, he abandons his duty and goes away to find out whether it is possible for him to forget.
characters.name: Death

characters.description: Duke of Sto Helit, and Susan's father. Once a farm boy taken on as Death's apprentice, he left that service to marry Death's adopted daughter Ysabell and to rule a small, prosperous duchy. He and his wife raised Susan deliberately as an ordinary child, telling her nothing whatever about where the family came from.
characters.name: Mort

characters.description: A young harpist from Llamedos, a wet and rocky country of rain, druids and bards, who has left home against his father's wishes to make a living from music in the city. Earnest, gentle and entirely without worldly sense, he believes that music matters more than anything else, which is a more dangerous position than he understands. His name means bud of the holly.
characters.name: Imp y Celyn

characters.description: A dwarf horn player in Ankh-Morpork, short of money, short of patience and short of most other things. He is the practical member of any group he joins, permanently concerned with where the next meal is coming from, and a competent musician who has never come close to being a famous one.
characters.name: Glod Glodsson

characters.description: A troll musician who makes his rhythms by striking rocks, and who has been scraping a living in the city's less rewarding venues. Slow, amiable and considerably shrewder than he appears, he adopts a shorter stage name once the band starts getting noticed.
characters.name: Lias Bluestone

characters.description: Death's servant, an elderly, dry, permanently disapproving man who keeps the house, cooks, and has run the domestic side of the Duty for a very long time. He was once a wizard, and he has excellent reasons for staying exactly where he is. He is alarmed by his master's disappearance and knows better than most what it will cost.
characters.name: Albert

characters.description: The rodent branch of the Duty, a skeletal rat in a small black robe carrying a small scythe, who collects the souls of rats and takes a keen interest in matters well outside that remit. He communicates entirely in squeaks and is a great deal more effective than his size suggests.
characters.name: The Death of Rats

characters.description: A talking raven who acts as interpreter for the Death of Rats, in exchange for a diet he describes at length and nobody wants to hear about. He is opinionated, easily offended, and extremely reluctant to say a certain word aloud.
characters.name: Quoth

characters.description: The Archchancellor of Unseen University, loud, hearty and impatient with anything requiring a committee. He notices that something is affecting his wizards and objects to it chiefly on the grounds of the noise and the embarrassment.
characters.name: Mustrum Ridcully

characters.description: Ankh-Morpork's most enterprising street trader, who has failed at more industries than most people have heard of and has never once been discouraged. He recognises the new music as the largest opportunity of his career and appoints himself the band's manager, with contracts written in his own favour and merchandise ready before the first performance is over.
characters.name: Cut-Me-Own-Throat Dibbler

characters.description: A senior wizard of Unseen University, elderly, portly and entirely conventional, until the new music reaches the faculty. He then develops opinions about hair, leather and rebellion that are new to him and deeply distressing to the Archchancellor.
characters.name: The Dean

characters.description: A young, practical wizard of Unseen University who does most of the faculty's actual thinking and is the only member of it inclined to investigate a phenomenon rather than shout at it. He works out rather more about what the music is than anyone wants to hear.
characters.name: Ponder Stibbons

characters.description: The secretary of the Guild of Musicians, who controls who is allowed to play for money in Ankh-Morpork and enforces it rigorously. Small-minded, procedural and absolutely certain of his own authority, he regards unlicensed musicians as a threat to the trade and is prepared to go a long way to remove one.
characters.name: Mr Clete

characters.description: The orangutan keeper of Unseen University's library, who turns out to be a capable pianist when the occasion demands it, and who is not remotely self-conscious about joining in.
characters.name: The Librarian

recaps.ending: Death comes back. His attempt to forget fails, because forgetting is the one thing he cannot do, and he returns to find his granddaughter standing between the music and the boy it intends to use up. The Music With Rocks In has arranged Buddy's death to complete him as a legend, and Susan cannot hold it off alone. Death confronts the music directly, drives it out of the guitar and out of the world, and then does what he did once before for the sake of someone he cared about: he reaches back and puts the accident right, so that Imp y Celyn lives. The music leaves the Disc and goes looking for somewhere else, leaving only echoes behind, and the guitar is destroyed. Imp survives with his life ahead of him and goes home to Llamedos; Glod and Cliff come out of it intact and better off than they started; Dibbler, having sold everything a fashion could be printed on, moves on to his next enterprise. Death takes back the Duty and, as a kindness, removes Susan's memory of Buddy and of the whole affair, returning her to school and to an ordinary life. The kindness is imperfect: she is still who she is, she still cannot always be seen when she does not wish to be, and traces of what happened remain.
recaps.in_short: When Susan Sto Helit's parents are killed in a coach accident, Death, who is her grandfather, cannot bear it and abandons his duty to go away and try to forget. Susan, sixteen and rigorously sensible, is fetched from boarding school by Albert and the Death of Rats and made to take up the Duty in his place. At the same time a young harpist from Llamedos, Imp y Celyn, arrives in Ankh-Morpork, is refused a licence by the Guild of Musicians, and buys an ancient guitar from a shop that is not there the next day. The guitar carries the Music With Rocks In, a force older than the Disc that uses musicians and discards them. With the dwarf Glod and the troll Cliff, Imp becomes Buddy of the Band With Rocks In; the music sweeps the city, infects the wizards, and makes Cut-Me-Own-Throat Dibbler rich. Susan discovers that Buddy should already be dead and that the music is keeping him alive for its own ends, and repeatedly intervenes. At the climax Death returns, drives the music out of the world, and restores Imp's life, then takes Susan's memory of it and sends her back to school.

recaps.text: Previously: Death is the robed skeleton who collects the souls of the dying, and he has been curious about the living for a very long time. He once took on a farm boy named Mort as his apprentice, and when the arrangement ended badly he set matters right at his own cost, dismissed the boy from his service, and gave him his blessing to marry Ysabell, the daughter Death had adopted and raised in his house. Mort became Duke of Sto Helit and the two had a daughter. Later, Death was briefly relieved of his office altogether and spent a season living as a mortal farmhand under the name Bill Door, harvesting a field and learning, at first hand, what it is to have a limited amount of time and to lose people. He fought to get his duty back and won it. From that period there also remains a small subordinate, the Death of Rats. Death returned to his work permanently changed, and permanently attached to the living in a way his office does not allow for.

Mort, Duke of Sto Helit, and his wife Ysabell are killed when their coach goes off a road in a storm. Death, who is Ysabell's father and therefore the girl's grandfather, cannot accept it, and the loss is worse for him because he forgets nothing, ever. Rather than continue, he walks away from the Duty entirely and goes away in search of a way to forget, which for him has never been possible and which he intends to attempt anyway. Their daughter Susan, sixteen years old, is left at the Quirm College for Young Ladies, where she has always been an awkward pupil: sharply logical, difficult to teach anything she considers untrue, and possessed of abilities she has never thought worth mentioning, including the knack of not being noticed. Meanwhile, in the rainy land of Llamedos, a young harpist named Imp y Celyn quarrels with his father and sets out for Ankh-Morpork to make a living from music.

With Death gone, the Duty is going undone, and Albert and the Death of Rats come to fetch Susan. Binky, Death's horse, takes her out into a world where she can see lifetimers running out and is expected to be present when they do. She resists, argues, and starts doing the work anyway. In Ankh-Morpork, Imp discovers that playing for money requires a Guild of Musicians licence he cannot afford, and falls in with two other unlicensed players: Glod Glodsson, a dwarf horn player, and Lias Bluestone, a troll who drums on rocks. When Imp's harp is destroyed in a brawl he buys a replacement from a small shop in an alley, an old guitar priced at a dozen dollars, and the shop is not there when he goes back. The instrument is far older than it looks, and playing it produces a music nobody on the Disc has heard before.

The Band With Rocks In begins to play, and the effect on audiences is immediate and physical. The music spreads through Ankh-Morpork faster than any fashion: young people change how they dress and speak, crowds form wherever the band appears, and the sound gets into places it has no business being, including Unseen University, where the Dean acquires a leather jacket and opinions and the Archchancellor's authority stops working. Cut-Me-Own-Throat Dibbler appoints himself manager, renames Imp as Buddy, and has merchandise on sale before the audience has left. Susan, working the Duty, encounters Buddy and finds something wrong with him that she cannot explain, and finds herself unwilling to do what the job requires. The Death of Rats and a foul-tempered raven take an unhelpful interest in her decisions.

Susan learns what is actually happening. Buddy's life should already have ended, and it is the music that is keeping him going, because it wants a player and intends to keep this one until it has finished with him. The Music With Rocks In is not a style but a thing: older than the Disc, drifting between worlds, it takes hold of musicians, drives them to play, makes them briefly enormous, and uses them up. Susan begins deliberately intervening to keep Buddy alive, which is precisely the abuse of the Duty that ended her father's apprenticeship. Albert warns her where it leads. Far away, Death has enlisted in the Klatchian Foreign Legion, an outfit whose members have all joined in order to forget and have all forgotten what it was, and his own experiment is failing, because he is constitutionally incapable of forgetting anything and drink does nothing to a body with no chemistry to affect. At the University, Ponder Stibbons works out more about the phenomenon than anyone wants to hear.

The band becomes the largest thing in the city. Imitators appear everywhere, the wizards form an ensemble of their own, and the Librarian is recruited to a piano when one is needed. This brings the Guild of Musicians down on them: its secretary, Mr Clete, cannot license the band, cannot control it, and cannot tolerate it, and he arranges for the problem to be removed by people who do that professionally. Dibbler, meanwhile, is thinking bigger, and announces a free festival, an event on a scale nobody has attempted, with the band at the centre of it. Susan keeps standing between Buddy and the end of his life, and the music keeps arranging opportunities. Death, having failed entirely to forget, begins the journey back.

The free festival happens, an enormous crowd and the band at the height of what the music can make of them, and afterwards the tour continues because the music will not let it stop. The pattern it wants is clear enough: a musician who burns very brightly and then dies young becomes permanent, and the music has arranged such endings before. It sets up an accident on the road for Buddy that mirrors the one that killed Susan's parents. Susan reaches him and holds the moment open, but she is a sixteen-year-old standing against something that has crossed between worlds and has done this many times before, and holding it is all she can do. It is at this point that Death, having discovered that the one thing he cannot do is forget, comes back to take up his own duty.

Death confronts the music itself, forces it out of the guitar and out of the world, and destroys the instrument; the music leaves the Disc to look for another one, and only echoes of it remain behind. He then reaches back and undoes the accident, so that Imp y Celyn lives, and the arrangement he made for his daughter's husband long ago is quietly repeated for his granddaughter's sake. Imp goes home to Llamedos with his life restored. Glod and Cliff survive the whole business better off than they began it, and Dibbler, having sold everything the fashion could be printed on, turns to his next enterprise. Death resumes the Duty. As a last kindness he takes away Susan's memory of Buddy and of everything that happened, and returns her to school and an ordinary life, though the kindness is incomplete: she is still her grandfather's granddaughter, still not always visible when she chooses otherwise, and something of the music, and of the boy, stays with her.

characters.description: Having left Sacred Valley behind, Lindon is a determined newcomer to the wider world, quickly confronted with how far his home's sacred arts lag behind everyone else's. Polite, calculating, and endlessly hungry to grow stronger, he is willing to study crafts and techniques that a proud sacred artist would consider beneath them. He throws himself into learning as a way to close the gap between himself and the powerful figures he now finds all around him, treating knowledge and adaptability as weapons in place of the inherited strength he lacks.
characters.name: Lindon

characters.description: Lindon's companion, a fierce and pragmatic sword artist from beyond Sacred Valley who is far more at home in the wider world than he is. Blunt and quick to fight, she is a formidable warrior for her level, though she must constantly manage the dangerous blood-madra presence bound to her by her late master's art. Loyal to Lindon and impatient with his caution, she pushes them both onward as they look for a place and a source of strength in an unfamiliar land.
characters.name: Yerin

characters.description: An elderly, sharp-tongued soulsmith who gets around on a spidery construct of mechanical legs and takes Lindon on as a student in the craft of building constructs from the remnants of dead sacred artists. Demanding and unsentimental, she gives Lindon his first real trade and a foundation of practical technique. Under her instruction he begins turning his knack for study into a genuine, marketable craft that sets him apart from ordinary fighters.
characters.name: Fisher Gesha

characters.description: A powerful young spear artist allied with the Sandviper sect, his face hidden behind bindings that conceal a curse-scarred visage. Skilled, proud, and driven, he seeks strength and standing, in large part to secure a future for his ailing younger sister. His ambitions and Lindon's repeatedly collide, making him one of Lindon's first serious rivals in the wider world.
characters.name: Jai Long

characters.description: Jai Long's younger sister, frail and often in poor health, whose wellbeing is the driving concern behind much of her brother's ambition. Gentle where he is hard, she gives his ruthless pursuit of power a sympathetic center and a reason beyond mere pride.
characters.name: Jai Chen

characters.description: The head of the Arelius family, a sacred artist of startling power who conceals his true strength behind a flamboyant, playful, and relentlessly meddlesome manner. Eithan takes an immediate interest in Lindon, seeing potential in him that others overlook, and draws both Lindon and Yerin into his family's orbit. Eccentric and impossible to predict, he becomes their patron and guide in the wider world, steering them toward opportunities and trouble in equal measure while keeping his true aims to himself.
characters.name: Eithan Arelius

characters.description: A capable and honorable retainer of the Arelius family who serves Eithan and helps oversee its affairs. Dutiful and skilled, he is at first uncertain what to make of Lindon, an outsider his eccentric lord has taken under his wing, but he judges people by their actions. He represents the disciplined, conventional side of the Arelius family that contrasts with Eithan's unpredictability.
characters.name: Cassias Arelius

recaps.ending: Soulsmith ends with Lindon and Yerin securely attached to Eithan Arelius and his family, having survived the contest over the Transcendent Ruins. Lindon emerges stronger, with new gains and a real trade in soulsmithing to complement his slowly growing Path, though he remains far weaker than the powers now around him. His rivalry with Jai Long, the masked Sandviper-allied spear artist, has hardened into a lasting enmity that is left unsettled, promising future conflict. In Eithan the pair have found a powerful, unpredictable patron who sees more in Lindon than anyone else and who intends to guide his growth for reasons of his own. As the book closes, Lindon and Yerin stand ready to move deeper into the powerful realm beyond the frontier under Eithan's wing, their sights set on challenges and strength far beyond anything the Desolate Wilds could offer.
recaps.in_short: Now in the wider world, Lindon and Yerin discover how far behind Sacred Valley truly was and search the rough frontier of the Desolate Wilds for strength and a place to belong. Lindon apprentices under the demanding old soulsmith Fisher Gesha, learning to craft constructs from the remnants of dead sacred artists and turning study into a real trade. The two are drawn into the orbit of Eithan Arelius, the eccentric, startlingly powerful head of the Arelius family, who sees rare potential in Lindon. They also make an enemy of Jai Long, a masked young spear artist driven by ambition and by concern for his ailing sister, Jai Chen. When the treasure-filled Transcendent Ruins open, the region's factions race to claim them, and Lindon joins the dangerous contest to gain the power he needs. The book ends with Lindon and Yerin coming through the struggle strengthened and firmly established under Eithan's patronage, their rivalry with Jai Long unresolved and their ambitions aimed higher.

recaps.text: Previously: Wei Shi Lindon was born Unsouled in Sacred Valley, an isolated, backward land that mistook its weak sacred arts for the height of power, and he was treated as a worthless outcast despite his ambition and cleverness. A visit from Suriel, a being of vast power, showed him how small and doomed his home truly was and challenged him to grow strong enough to matter. Refusing the limits of his birth, Lindon gathered forbidden knowledge and began real cultivation, clashing with the valley's ruling powers. When the outsider Sword Sage and his disciple Yerin arrived, the resulting upheaval left Yerin without her master, and she and Lindon, recognizing a shared drive to become strong, joined forces. At the close of the first book, Lindon left Sacred Valley behind and stepped into the wider world for the first time, with Yerin at his side and no illusions about how far he had to climb.

Out in the wider world at last, Lindon and Yerin quickly learn how far behind Sacred Valley truly was, encountering sacred artists and powers that dwarf anything from home. Making their way through the rough frontier of the Desolate Wilds, they search for a place to belong and a source of strength, trading on Yerin's fighting skill and Lindon's cunning. Lindon is confronted with entirely new disciplines, including the craft of soulsmithing, the art of building useful constructs from the remnants left behind by dead sacred artists. Eager for any advantage, he sets out to learn it, seeing in a practical trade a way to grow that does not depend on the raw talent he was told he lacks. The pair begin to grasp the true scale of the world they have entered and the many rival factions competing within it.

Lindon becomes the student of Fisher Gesha, a demanding old soulsmith who gives him his first real trade and teaches him to craft constructs, turning his habit of relentless study into a genuine skill. The pair's fortunes shift again when they draw the attention of Eithan Arelius, the eccentric and startlingly powerful head of the Arelius family, who sees potential in Lindon that others miss and pulls both him and Yerin into his orbit. At the same time they run afoul of Jai Long, a masked and formidable young spear artist tied to the Sandviper sect, whose drive for power, much of it for the sake of his ailing sister Jai Chen, sets him on a collision course with Lindon. Amid the region's shifting alliances, Lindon keeps building his craft and his strength, aware that he remains far weaker than the figures now shaping his fate.

Word spreads that the Transcendent Ruins, an ancient site holding rare treasures and techniques, are opening, and the region's sects and families scramble to claim what lies inside. Lindon sees the Ruins as a chance to gain the resources and power he badly needs to close the gap between himself and everyone around him, and he throws himself into the contest despite the danger. The competition sharpens the rivalry with Jai Long and the Sandvipers and tests the new alliances Lindon and Yerin have formed under the Arelius family. Backed by Eithan's interest and Fisher Gesha's training, and relying on preparation and cleverness rather than brute strength, Lindon positions himself to take advantage of the opportunity, while Yerin's combat skill and her volatile blood-madra inheritance both come into play as the stakes rise.

By the book's end, the struggle over the Transcendent Ruins comes to a head, with Lindon and Yerin coming through it changed and strengthened. The clash with Jai Long and the Sandviper sect hardens into a lasting rivalry rather than a settled score, leaving Jai Long as an enemy Lindon will have to reckon with again.
